questions.question: An enterprise upgrades to WiFi 6E access points and clients gain access to a newly opened band of clean spectrum beyond the congested 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz allocations. Which band was added?
questions.explanation: WiFi 6E extends 802.11ax into the newly licensed 6 GHz spectrum (5.925-7.125 GHz), roughly doubling usable channels; 2.4 and 5 GHz were already in use.

questions.question: An 802.11ax access point transmits different data to three laptops simultaneously on the same channel by steering a separate spatial stream to each. Which technology enables this?
questions.explanation: Single-user MIMO feeds multiple streams to one device; serving several clients concurrently on the same channel requires multi-user beamforming across spatial streams - MU-MIMO.

questions.question: WiFi 6 lets one access point serve a thermostat and a laptop inside the same transmission by assigning each device different subcarrier groups called resource units. Which technique is this?
questions.explanation: Subdividing a channel's subcarriers into resource units allocated to different clients in one transmission is OFDMA - WiFi 6's upgrade over OFDM, where the whole channel went to one client at a time.

questions.question: Where 802.11ac's modulation carries 8 bits per symbol, 802.11ax raises this to 10 bits per symbol under good signal conditions. Which modulation does it introduce?
questions.explanation: Bits per symbol = log2(constellation size): 802.11ac's 256-QAM gives 8 bits, and 802.11ax's denser constellation needs 2^10 = 1024 points for 10 bits - 1024-QAM.

questions.question: A WLAN must prioritize voice frames using WMM access categories - the capability added by the amendment that first defined QoS for 802.11. Which amendment is it?
questions.explanation: 802.11e added QoS to Wi-Fi via EDCA access categories (voice, video, best effort, background), the basis of WMM certification used to prioritize latency-sensitive frames.

questions.question: Two clients cannot hear each other and keep colliding at the access point - a hidden-node problem. A short request-then-grant frame exchange reserves the medium before the real data is sent. Which mechanism is this?
questions.explanation: The sender first transmits a Request To Send, the AP answers Clear To Send audible to all hidden nodes, and the reservation prevents mid-transmission collisions under CSMA/CA.

questions.question: To cover a warehouse without running cable to each access point, several APs relay traffic for one another over wireless backhaul links into one unified network. Which topology is this?
questions.explanation: APs that interconnect wirelessly and forward each other's traffic form a mesh network; traditional WLANs instead wire every AP back to the distribution system.

questions.question: An 802.11ac access point is configured for maximum throughput by bonding channels into its widest contiguous spectrum allocation. What channel width does it use?
questions.explanation: 802.11ac supports 20/40/80/160 MHz widths; the maximum contiguous allocation is 160 MHz (or 80+80 non-contiguous), which roughly doubles the 80 MHz rate.

questions.question: Instead of radiating equally in all directions, an access point's phased antenna array steers signal energy toward a specific client, raising its SNR at the edge of coverage. Which technique is this?
questions.explanation: Adjusting phase across antenna elements so signals add constructively at the client is (transmit) beamforming; it focuses RF energy rather than broadcasting omnidirectionally.

questions.question: Rather than trusting the passphrase alone, an admin configures the access point's access list to admit only a printer whose burned-in hardware address has been whitelisted. Which method is this?
questions.explanation: Permitting or denying association based on a device's hardware (MAC) address is MAC filtering - a weak control alone since addresses can be spoofed, but it matches the described whitelist.

questions.question: WPA3-Personal resists offline dictionary attacks by deriving keys through a Dragonfly-based exchange instead of the old PSK four-way handshake. Which handshake is this?
questions.explanation: WPA3 replaces the offline-crackable PSK exchange with SAE - Simultaneous Authentication of Equals, a Dragonfly PAKE that adds forward secrecy and defeats passive dictionary attacks.

questions.question: An auditor cites the amendment that defined the Robust Security Network - CCMP/AES encryption and 802.1X authentication - which the WPA2 certification implements. Which amendment is it?
questions.explanation: IEEE 802.11i introduced the Robust Security Network framework (AES-CCMP, 802.1X/EAP); WPA2 is the Wi-Fi Alliance certification of that completed standard.

questions.question: A docking station pushes multi-gigabit traffic across a desk - about ten meters at most - using 60 GHz spectrum that walls easily block. Which WiGig standard is it?
questions.explanation: The 60 GHz band offers huge channels and multi-gigabit rates but propagates only a few meters indoors - the trade-off of 802.11ad, marketed as WiGig.

questions.question: Battery-powered sensors must transmit up to a kilometer on sub-1 GHz spectrum at modest data rates under the 'HaLow' design. Which 802.11 standard covers this?
questions.explanation: 802.11ah runs in sub-GHz spectrum where signals travel farther and penetrate better than 2.4 GHz, trading throughput for the long range and low power that IoT needs.

questions.question: Battery door sensors on WiFi 6 negotiate exact wake-up schedules with the access point and sleep in between to conserve power. Which feature is this?
questions.explanation: Target Wake Time lets 802.11ax clients agree on scheduled wake windows with the AP and doze between them, dramatically extending battery life for IoT devices.

questions.question: A site survey shows a client reading -90 dBm while working stations measure -60 dBm. What does the -90 dBm value indicate?
questions.explanation: dBm values closer to 0 are stronger; -90 dBm is near the noise floor and indicates marginal coverage.

questions.question: What is the maximum theoretical PHY data rate of 802.11n when using 40 MHz channels with four spatial streams?
questions.explanation: 802.11n reaches 150 Mbps per spatial stream at 40 MHz; four streams yield 600 Mbps.

questions.question: Analyzing a WPA2 capture, an analyst sees four EAPOL-Key frames exchanging nonces after authentication - the exchange an attacker can replay offline to test guesses against the PSK. Which handshake was captured?
questions.explanation: WPA2 derives the pairwise transient key from the PMK plus the ANonce/SNonce exchanged in the four EAPOL-Key messages; capturing them enables the classic offline PSK crack.

questions.question: An attacker sends forged management frames ordering a victim's client to disconnect from its access point, forcing it to roam to an evil twin. What attack is this?
questions.explanation: Unprotected management frames let an attacker spoof deauthentication frames, disconnecting clients so they reassociate to a rogue AP.

questions.question: Why do 2.4 GHz deployments restrict themselves to channels 1, 6, and 11 for co-located access points?
alternatives: their center frequencies are spaced far enough apart to avoid interference
questions.explanation: Each 2.4 GHz channel is 22 MHz wide but spaced only 5 MHz apart; only channels 1, 6, and 11 are far enough apart to avoid overlap.
